extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, teacher educators, and graduate students studying proof and proving in school and university mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic review protocol and coding scheme for mapping recent mathematics-education research on proof and proving using Cohen et al.'s instructional triangle; includes paper selection, focus coding, level and contribution classification, and thematic synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criteria for papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Considered all papers obtained from searching the journals in Table 1 that included proof, proving, or argumentation in at least one of their title/abstract/keywords and that were published (including ‘online first’) between 1/1/2018 and 1/6/2022 in the mathematics education research journals listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals were restricted to those graded A*, A, or B by the expert panel convened by EMS/ERME (Toerner & Arzarello, 2012). The decision was guided by a need for a systematic and practical procedure rather than elitism; the authors acknowledge that important work outside these limits (other journals, conferences, books, non-English) was excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion criteria for papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluded papers that were book reviews, science focused, or corrections/comments on other papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screening involved abstracts and often full texts to remove non-research items or items outside the topical focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional triangle focus categories (S, T, C, SC, ST, TC, STC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paper was categorized according to whether the paper’s (main) focus was on S (students), T (teacher), C (content), SC, ST, TC, or STC, following Cohen et al.’s triadic conceptualization of instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding rules/examples: if teacher is present but not prominent in analysis the paper is coded SC; if the paper focused on teachers' views while students' role was background it is TC; if both teacher's and students' roles were explicitly investigated code STC; if neither students nor teacher were crux of research questions (only content) code C; a paper investigating teacher-student interactions with content not playing a particular role is coded ST.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role assignment for participant-types (preservice teachers and mathematicians)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that examined (preservice) teachers as learners were categorized as S (their role in the educational system—university—is that of a student), whereas those that examined them as teachers of mathematics were categorized as T. Similarly, papers that examined mathematicians from their roles as instructors in university were categorized as T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign participant role based on their role in the educational system under study rather than job title alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational-level classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Recorded the educational level of each paper as school, university, both (school and university), or discipline (not concerned with a particular level but the discipline in general).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher education papers with preservice teachers were classified as university level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building ground vs Breaking ground (contribution classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: All papers were judged to make some theoretical and/or methodological contribution and were further classified as either building ground (further developing or implementing existing theoretical ideas, methods, or findings) or breaking ground (developing or implementing new theoretical ideas or methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking ground papers were coded further according to whether they explicitly made a theoretical and/or a methodological contribution (cf. Hanna & Knipping, 2020).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking ground chronological treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: For papers coming from the same group of authors making the same kind of methodological or theoretical contribution, only the first chronologically published item in the list was recorded as breaking ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow-up publications by the same group on the same contribution were recorded as building ground (strengthening/elaborating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding procedure and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Two of the authors considered all categorizations separately and then resolved all disagreements through discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter-rater agreement was reported (initial Kappa = 0.718); the authors note inter-rater agreement was not a major concern for this review but report the statistic as evidence of 'good' to 'excellent' initial agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Cohen et al.'s triadic conceptualization as organizing framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopted Cohen et al.’s (2003) notion of the instructional triangle according to which instruction 'consists of interactions among teachers and students around content, in environments' as the organizing conceptual framework for the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framework draws attention to the main actors—teacher (T) and students (S)—and the content (C), and to the relationships among them. The authors acknowledge limitations of using the 'simple' triangle but judged it appropriate for a bird’s-eye review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus-coding practical examples and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational rules clarifying borderline cases: e.g., if teacher present in classroom discussions but not featured prominently in analysis, code SC; if teacher’s and students’ roles both explicitly investigated code STC; if students and teacher presence missing code C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete examples were provided to improve coding consistency across papers with complex designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic grouping/inductive theme identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Within each instructional-triangle category the authors inductively identified themes (e.g., role of examples, understandings of proof, technological environments) and selected papers to illustrate those themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theme identification was inductive and to some extent subjective; selection of illustrative papers aimed for representation of themes, authors, and emerging trends but was influenced by subjective judgment and constraints on how many papers could be referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative distribution metrics used in synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarized and analyzed counts/distributions of the 103 papers by focus (S, T, C, SC, ST, TC, STC), by educational level (school/university/both/discipline), and by contribution type (breaking vs building ground); presented in Tables 2 and 3 and discussed in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used these counts to derive observations (e.g., almost half of papers were SC; 20 papers judged breaking ground with counts by category).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for coding a paper as making a theoretical and/or methodological contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A breaking ground paper was coded as theoretical and/or methodological if it explicitly made a theoretical and/or methodological contribution as stated in the paper (the authors followed Hanna & Knipping, 2020, for the distinction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a paper explicitly introduced new theoretical constructs or new methodological approaches it was flagged as breaking ground and assigned the appropriate subtype(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic/theme categories used to characterize research content
rubrics_metrics.description: The review used a set of recurring thematic topics to describe and cluster papers (examples: role and use of examples / counterexamples; participants’ understandings and conceptions of proof; technological environments supporting proof; proof writing and reading; prospective teachers’ proof constructions and evaluations; affective aspects; teacher content knowledge and perspectives; teacher interactions with proof-related tasks; teaching approaches; proof norms and criteria; novel theoretical/methodological frameworks; linguistic and discursive aspects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These themes function as content-focused classification labels to summarize what kind of questions and methods papers in each instructional-triangle category pursued; the authors discuss representative papers under these themes and note relative frequencies (e.g., many SC papers addressed examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of evidence about authenticity and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that problematized methods used to gain insights into mathematical practice (e.g., Mejía-Ramos & Weber, 2020) were used to set criteria for caution when inferring instructional implications from certain research methods (e.g., task-based interviews with mathematicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological caution: the authors recommend considering limitations of lab-based task methods and complementing them with other methods to make valid claims about authentic mathematical practice and its instructional implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of limitations and scope choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The review explicitly documents its scope limitations (journal selection, time period, exclusion of conference proceedings and non-English papers) and explains these choices as methodological constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors recommend awareness that different inclusion choices (e.g., adding conference proceedings or other journals) could produce a different mapping; this transparency is part of the review protocol.
